exp.1:17:
God asks his people to stop and think, to set their hearts, that is, their attention and their minds, on this day and from now on. He points them to a precise date: the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, when the foundation of the temple was being laid. He asks them to consider what has happened and what is coming.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, after the return from exile in Babylon. The people had left the temple half-built while they took care of their own houses. Because of this, their harvests were yielding very little. God calls them to turn back to him and promises that, from that day on, he will bless them.

Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our lives. Take a few minutes this week to think calmly about whether you are giving God the place that belongs to him, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.1:6:
It says that God will shake all the nations. Then the one "desired by all nations" will come, and God will fill this house with his glory. "I will fill" means "I will fill," and "nations" are the peoples or nations of the earth. About "the desired one" there are two readings: some believe it refers to the Messiah, Jesus; others hold that it speaks of the riches and treasures of the nations, which would come to the temple, as the following verse suggests.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai, around 520 B.C. The people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, but they felt discouraged because it seemed poor compared with the earlier one. God asks them not to fear and reminds them that his Spirit is with them.

When your work seems small or fragile, do not lose heart. God is sovereign over the whole world and keeps his promises. Keep serving him with confidence, because his presence matters more than appearances.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that God spoke through the prophet Haggai on a precise date: the first day of the sixth month of the second year of King Darius. The message was for two leaders: Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, and Joshua, the high priest. The phrase "by the hand of the prophet" means that God spoke through him.

Haggai speaks after the Jews had returned from exile in Babylon. That date corresponds, according to most scholars, to the year 520 B.C. The temple in Jerusalem was still not rebuilt. God addresses the civil and religious leaders first, because they had the responsibility to guide the people. What follows shows that the people were saying it was still not the time to rebuild.

For today: God speaks at specific moments and expects a response. Let's stop postponing what He asks of us. If you have responsibility toward others, start today with one small step of obedience.
exp.0:4:
God asks his people to stop and think seriously about how they are living. The phrase "Consider your ways" means reflecting carefully, and "ways" refers to the conduct, decisions, and priorities of each day.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, after the people had returned from exile in Babylon. They were busy with their own houses, which were finished and paneled with wood, while the temple still lay in ruins. God shows them that, despite all their effort, they were living with want and dissatisfaction.

For today: before we keep rushing after our goals, it is wise to pause and ask whether God holds first place in our time, money, and energy. A sincere moment of prayer can help us put in order what matters most.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells us that the leaders and all the people listened to God through the prophet Haggai. Zerubbabel was the governor, and Joshua was the high priest. They did not only hear the words; they received them as coming from God, and the people had a deep respect for the Lord, taking his message seriously.

God was speaking through Haggai to the Jews who had returned from exile. They had devoted themselves to their own houses and had left the rebuilding of the temple on hold. God had shown them that the drought and the shortage were tied to that wrong priority. Here we see the response: obedience, not just listening.

Today, when God speaks to us through his Word, we can respond with humility and not with excuses. Ask yourself what area of your life you have put ahead of God, and take one concrete step to correct it.
exp.1:9:
This verse marks the date of a new message: the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of King Darius. It says that "the word of the Lord" came "by Haggai the prophet," meaning God spoke through him. It is an introduction to what follows.

Haggai spoke to the people who had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. Shortly before, God had promised that his presence and peace would be with them. Now God tells them to ask the priests about the law, to teach the people something about holiness and obedience.

For today: God speaks at concrete moments in our lives. Set aside a fixed time to listen to his Word, and ask him what he wants to teach you today.
exp.1:15:
It says that, before the work on the temple was resumed, the people expected a great deal and received little. They would go to a heap of grain that was supposed to yield twenty measures (a measure of grain) and would find only ten. They would go to the winepress (where the grapes are trodden) expecting fifty jars of wine, and would come away with only twenty.

The prophet Haggai speaks on God's behalf to the people who had returned from exile. They had left the temple in ruins while they attended to their own houses and harvests. God asks them to remember how things went for them during that time and to see the connection between their neglect and their scarcity. The verses that follow say that God had struck them with blight, but they did not turn back to him.

For today: it is worth examining what holds first place in our lives. If we seek God first, we can trust that he will care for everything else. Without him, our effort may leave us empty.
exp.1:12:
He says that Haggai asks the priests what happens if a person made unclean by touching a dead body touches something, such as bread, wine, or oil. The priests answer that this food becomes unclean. "Unclean" means defiled according to the law, and "food" is what people eat.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai to the people who returned from exile. They had set aside the rebuilding of the temple and were busy with their own houses. With this teaching from the law, God shows that holiness is not easily passed on, but uncleanness is. Thus, their offerings and labors were not acceptable as long as their hearts had not turned back to God. Some interpreters explain this in slightly different ways, but the central idea is that one.

Today we can remember that it is not enough to do religious things if the heart is far from God. It is good to ask ourselves, with humility, which priorities we should put in order so that we place Him first.
exp.1:5:
God says that within a short time he will shake everything: the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land. "Yet once, it is a little while" means "within a little while." "The dry land" is the solid ground, in contrast with the sea. It is a way of saying that God will shake all creation.

The Lord of hosts speaks, through the prophet Haggai, to a people who had returned from exile and felt discouraged while rebuilding the temple. God calls them to be strong and not to fear, because he is with them. The verse that follows speaks of the nations and of the glory of the house. Some see it fulfilled in part in history, and others connect it with Christ; interpreters understand it in several ways.

For today: when everything seems unstable or your effort seems small, remember that God rules even what is shaken. Keep serving him with confidence, because he is with you.
exp.0:6:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, calls his people to stop and think seriously about the way they are living. The word "Consider" means to reflect, to think over carefully. "Your ways" refers to their decisions, priorities and habits.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai to the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon. They had left the rebuilding of the temple unfinished and were busy with their own houses. God shows them that, although they worked hard, nothing brought them satisfaction: they sowed, ate, drank and clothed themselves, but always felt that something was lacking.

For today: pause and review your priorities. Ask yourself whether you are putting God last while you run after your own concerns. You can begin by giving him your time, your attention and the best of your strength.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that the rain stopped falling from the sky and that the land did not give its crops. "Stayed" means held back or restrained. "Fruit" refers to the crops, what the earth produces for food.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai to the people of Judah, who had returned from exile. They were busy building and decorating their own houses, while the temple still lay in ruins. God explains to them that the scarcity they were suffering was connected to that misplaced priority. When they heard it, the people and their leaders responded with reverent fear and obedience.

For today: it is worth asking what place God holds in our priorities. We can begin the day by seeking Him first, and trusting that He cares for what we need. This does not mean that every hardship is a punishment, since the Bible shows that there are many causes.
exp.1:2:
God asks who among those present still saw the temple in its first glory, that is, Solomon's temple. Then he asks them to compare that with what they see now. The phrase "in your eyes" in the verse means "as you see it now." The phrase "as nothing" means that it seems very small and without value to them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Haggai, a few years after the return from exile in Babylon. He addresses Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the people. The new temple looked poor beside the former one, and the people were discouraged. God names that sadness in order to encourage them, and right away he tells them: "be strong... for I am with you."

For today: sometimes we compare what we do with greater things and become discouraged. God does not measure the value of your work by its size, but by his presence with you. Keep obeying, even when it looks small.
exp.1:8:
The explanation says that the temple, called the "latter" one, meaning the last or the most recent, will have more glory than the first. God himself guarantees this and adds that he will give peace in that place. The explanation also notes that the name "Lord of hosts" refers to the Lord as almighty God.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai, around the year 520 B.C. The Jews had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, but it was modest compared with Solomon's, and the people were growing discouraged. God reminds them that the gold and the silver are his, and promises to fill the house with glory. Some understand this as referring to the temple of that time; others also see a promise that points to Christ, "the Desire of all nations."

For today: do not be discouraged if what you do for God seems small. Stay faithful, because he can give glory and peace where you see little.
exp.0:3:
God asks the people a direct question: does it seem like the right time for them to live comfortably in houses with walls covered in wood, while the temple still lies in ruins?

The word "ruins" here means abandoned, in ruins.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Haggai. The Jews had returned from exile in Babylon and had begun rebuilding the temple, but they left the work stopped. They said it was not yet the time, and meanwhile they busied themselves fixing up their own houses.

For today: it is worth reviewing our priorities. It is not wrong to care for the home, but we can ask ourselves whether we are putting God off until later. A simple step is to set aside a fixed time today to pray, read the Bible, or serve in your church.
exp.1:21:
God announces that he is going to bring down the power of the nations. "Overthrow" means to turn over or bring down. The "throne of the kingdoms" and the "chariots" with their horses represent political and military strength. The ending says that the enemy soldiers will strike each other down, each one by the sword of his brother, meaning they will fall into confusion and violence.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Haggai around 520 B.C. He speaks to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, when the people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. They were small and weak in the face of empires. God reminds them that he is above all human power. The verse that follows shows that Zerubbabel is protected by God, like a seal of authority.

For today: when the world seems dominated by frightening powers, remember that God is still the King. Trust him and keep faithfully doing what he has entrusted to you.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that God spoke again through the prophet Haggai, on the twenty-first day of the seventh month. "The word of the Lord by the prophet" means that God sent his message using Haggai as his spokesman.

The message comes from God. Haggai spoke to the Jews who had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. According to the book, this date is about a month after they resumed the work. Many people judged the new temple to look poor compared with the former one, and discouragement was strong. God sends this word to encourage them.

God still speaks to his people in times of weariness or discouragement. When your work for him seems small, open his Word and listen. His encouragement does not depend on what you see, but on his presence with you.
exp.1:20:
God asks Haggai to speak to Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, and to announce that He will shake the heavens and the earth. The phrase "shake the heavens and the earth" describes a huge upheaval that shows God's power over everything He has created.

Jehovah speaks through the prophet Haggai after the people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. Zerubbabel was the leader of that small and fragile people. God reminds him that He rules over the kingdoms and that the powers of this world do not have the final word. The verses that follow confirm this: God has chosen Zerubbabel and watches over him.

For today: when the world seems unstable or powerful people intimidate you, remember that God is still in control. You can keep faithfully doing what He has entrusted to you, trusting that your life is in His hands.
exp.0:13:
God himself, the explanation says, stirred the hearts of the leaders and of all the people so that they set to work. To "stir up the spirit" means that God encouraged them from within, giving them desire and courage. The governor was the civil authority, and the high priest was the religious leader. "Came and did work" means that they arrived and began building the temple.

The prophet Haggai speaks to the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon. They had left the rebuilding of the temple unfinished for some years. God told them, "I am with you," and they answered with reverence and obedience. This took place during the reign of Darius, about 520 years before Christ.

For today: when God moves you to do something good, do not wait until you feel perfect. Ask him to awaken your heart, trust that he is with you, and take the first step.
exp.1:11:
This verse describes a question about the law. If someone carries holy meat, set apart for worship, in the edge of his clothing, and with that edge touches bread, stew, wine, oil or any other food, does that food become holy? The priests answer that it does not. The "skirt" is the fold of the garment, and "food" here means prepared food.

God speaks through the prophet Haggai in the second year of King Darius. The people had returned from exile, but they were slow to rebuild the temple. God uses this question to show that holiness is not passed on automatically, while impurity is, as the following verses say.

For today: being religiously active is not enough to be holy. God looks at the heart and at obedience. Today you can ask him to cleanse you and help you put him first.
exp.0:7:
God tells the Israelites to go up into the hills, bring back timber, and rebuild the temple. He promises that he will take pleasure in that work and that he will be honored. "House" refers to the temple, and the sense of the phrase "I will take pleasure in it" is that God will accept the work with delight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, after the people's return from exile in Babylon. The people had been busy with their own houses and had left the temple in ruins. Because of this, their efforts produced little, and God calls them to reflect and to put first what matters to him.

Today we can ask ourselves what we have put off in our life with God. Perhaps it is prayer, church, or service to others. Take one concrete first step this week, and trust that he will take care of the rest.
exp.1:18:
God asks whether there is still seed left in the barn. That is, almost nothing is stored away. Besides this, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate and the olive tree have not yet produced fruit. Yet God promises: "from this day will I bless you."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Haggai, a few months after the people returned from exile. They had neglected to rebuild the temple, and God had corrected them with poor harvests. Now, on the day the foundations are laid, He asks them to set their hearts on Him and promises that His blessing begins.

For today: when everything seems scarce, put God first and obey what He has already shown you. Trust that He cares for you, even when you do not yet see the fruit.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that God spoke a second time to the prophet Haggai that same day, on the twenty-fourth day of the month. It is only an introduction: it marks that a second message is coming.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Haggai. The people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. That same day, God had already promised them blessing. Now he adds a word for Zerubbabel, the governor, with a promise about his authority over the kingdoms. Scholars agree on the context, though they debate how that final promise is fulfilled.

For today: God does not stop at a single word of encouragement, but keeps speaking to those who obey him. If you have taken a step of faith, even if you do not yet see fruit, keep listening for his voice and trust that he has more to say to you.
exp.1:16:
God reminds them that he struck them with the scorching east wind (a dry, burning wind from the desert), with blight (a fungus that ruins the wheat), and with hail, damaging all the work of their hands. Even so, the people did not return to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, around the year 520 B.C. The Jews had come back from exile, but they left the rebuilding of the temple on hold while they looked after their own houses. God points out to them that their poor harvests were a warning. Right after this, he promises blessing from the day they resumed the work.

For today: when things go wrong again and again, it is worth stopping and asking ourselves humbly whether God is inviting us to come back to him. Not every hardship is a punishment, but it is always a good time to put God first again.
exp.0:1:
God speaks through the prophet Haggai and quotes what the people were saying: "The time has not yet come to rebuild the temple." The phrase "Lord of hosts" is a title that shows God as Lord over all power.

The temple in Jerusalem was in ruins. The Jews had returned from exile in Babylon, during the reign of the Persian king Darius, and had begun the work, but it had stopped. God speaks to Zerubbabel, the governor, and to Joshua, the high priest, and shows that the people were using the waiting as an excuse. The verses that follow confront them for caring for their own houses.

Today we can ask ourselves what thing of God we are leaving for "later." Perhaps it is prayer, service, or reconciling with someone. Today we can take one concrete step, small but real.
exp.0:5:
It says that the people worked hard, yet very little came of it. They sowed a good deal and harvested little; they ate and drank without being satisfied; they dressed themselves and still were cold. The phrase about storing the harvest refers to keeping the crop in the barn. The worker paid by the day is the one who earns wages by the day, and the image of a bag with holes means the money slipped right through.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. They were busy with their well-built houses, while the temple still lay in ruins. God calls them to reflect on their priorities. Many understand that scarcity as a consequence of having put him in second place.

For today: review where you invest your time, your money, and your strength. Ask God whether he holds first place, and take one concrete step to put him there.
exp.0:12:
Here the prophet Haggai, sent by God, gives the people a brief message: "I am with you." This means "I am with you."

The people had returned from exile in Babylon, but they had left the rebuilding of the temple abandoned. God had spoken to them with firmness, and they, together with their leaders Zerubbabel and Joshua, recognized his voice and felt reverent fear. Then, instead of more rebuke, God gives them a promise: his presence. After this, he himself stirs up their spirit, and they begin to work.

When God corrects us, he does not do so to reject us, but to encourage us to return to him. If there is something you have left unfinished in your spiritual life, begin today with a small step, trusting that God goes with you.
exp.1:3:
God speaks to three groups: to Zerubbabel, the governor; to Joshua, the high priest; and to all the people. He says the same thing to all three: be strong, take courage, and work. The reason is that God himself is with them. The word "strong" means being firm and courageous. The title "LORD of hosts" speaks of God's power over all things.

This was said to the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon to rebuild the temple. The elders remembered the earlier temple, which was far more beautiful, and the new one seemed to them like nothing at all. They were discouraged. God encourages them to continue, reminding them of his covenant and his presence.

For today: when what you do seems small or weak compared with other things, do not stop. Keep working in faith, because God is with you, and he values your obedience more than the results you can see.
exp.1:1:
God asks Haggai to speak to three groups: Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah; Joshua, the high priest; and the rest of the people. The word "Speak" is a command, and the old spelling of the word "to" appears twice in the verse as a plain connecting word.

The one speaking is the LORD, and He does so through the prophet Haggai. The Jews had returned from exile and were working to rebuild the temple. As time passed, the work seemed small compared with the former temple, and discouragement grew. God first addresses the leaders and then everyone, because the task belonged to all of them.

For today: when what you are doing seems small or unremarkable, remember that God sees you and speaks to you personally. Be faithful in the part that is yours, whether leading, serving, or supporting, and trust that He is with you.
exp.1:7:
He says that all the silver and all the gold in the world belong to God. He is the one speaking, called "the Lord of hosts," that is, the Lord who rules over every power. "The silver is mine" means "it belongs to me."

Haggai spoke to the Jews who had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. It was a modest temple, and the elders sadly remembered the splendor of the earlier one. God encouraged them: he did not need their wealth, because everything is his, and he himself would fill the house with glory. Christians have seen in the "desire of all nations" a reference to Christ, although some interpret it in other ways.

For today: if God owns everything, you do not have to live in fear of scarcity. Give with confidence, serve with what you have, and do not become discouraged if your work seems small. God knows how to make it great.
exp.1:4:
God reminds his people of the covenant he made with them when they came out of Egypt. He says that, just as then, his Spirit remains among them. For this reason he commands them: "fear ye not." Old words: "covenanted" means "agreed to or established"; "ye" is "you."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Haggai, around 520 BC. A group of Jews had returned from exile and was rebuilding the temple. Many were losing heart, because this temple seemed small and poor compared with the former one. God encourages Zerubbabel, Joshua, and all the people to keep working.

Today, when what we do seems small or insufficient, we can remember that God is faithful to his promises and is present. His companionship is worth more than our resources. We can keep serving with confidence, without letting fear or comparison stop us.
exp.0:8:
God says the people "look for much," that is, they expect large harvests and profits, but they "find little." What they bring home, God "blows upon," as if the wind carried it off and it vanished. "Hurries to his own house" means that each one rushes to take care of his own affairs. The reason is that God's house, the temple, remains "desolate," that is, in ruins.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, around the year 520 BC. The Jews had returned from exile in Babylon, but they left the rebuilding of the temple on hold while they raised and repaired their own homes. God calls them to reflect on their priorities.

For today: review what holds first place in your time, your money, and your strength. Putting God first does not guarantee wealth, but it orders the heart and gives meaning to what we do.
exp.1:13:
It says that the people, with everything they did and offered, were unclean before God. The prophet's name appears in the source as Haggeo, which is Haggai. Unclean means impure, not fit for God. The explanation also notes that the people's offerings did not please God, even though they kept offering sacrifices.

Haggai speaks in the name of the Lord to the Jews who had returned from exile. They had stopped rebuilding the temple in order to attend to their own houses. The priests had just confirmed that holiness does not spread from one thing to another, but uncleanness does. So their offerings could not make them clean while their hearts were careless. Some scholars debate who is meant by "this people," but the context points to those who had slowed down the work.

For today: performing religious rituals is not enough if we put God in last place. Examine your priorities and, if needed, return to obeying Him with a sincere heart, starting with what He has asked of you.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that God spoke again, and he did so through the prophet Haggai. That means God used the prophet as a messenger to deliver his word. The text says "Then came the word of the Lord," so the message comes directly from God and is delivered through Haggai.

The context is that the people had returned from exile in Babylon. For years they had left the rebuilding of the temple undone, and they were saying that the time had not yet come. God sends Haggai to speak to the governor Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua, and through them to all the people. The next verse shows God's complaint: they were tending their own houses, but the house of God lay in ruins.

For today: do not keep postponing what God has asked of you with excuses like "the time is not right." Ask him what place it has in your priorities, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.0:14:
This verse gives only a date: the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius. It is the day the people began to work on the house of God. "Governor" was the civil authority, and "high priest" was the religious leader.

Haggai was a prophet who spoke on God's behalf to the Jews who had returned from exile. They had left the rebuilding of the temple undone for years. God told them, "I am with you," and stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, of Joshua, and of all the people. According to the text, the work was resumed about three weeks after Haggai's first word (1:1), although the exact count depends on how the calendar is read. King Darius refers to the king of Persia.

For today: when God moves you to do something good, do not put it off. Begin today, even with a small step, trusting that He is with you.
exp.1:10:
God tells the prophet Haggai to ask the priests a question about the law. Here "law" means the instruction or teaching of God about what is clean and what is unclean. The words "Thus saith the Lord of hosts" mean: "This is what the Lord, the God of the heavenly armies, says."

God speaks through the prophet Haggai in the year 520 BC, about three months after the rebuilding of the temple had resumed. The priests were the teachers responsible for explaining what was clean and what was not. God uses their answers to show the people a lesson about their spiritual condition.

For today: before asking for blessings, it is good to ask ourselves whether our heart is clean before God. We can pray sincerely, ask him for forgiveness, and obey him in concrete matters, trusting that his grace can indeed cleanse us.
exp.1:14:
God tells the people to think carefully and reflect. To "consider" means to pay close attention and meditate. He asks them to look back at how things went for them before they began rebuilding the temple, "from before a stone was laid upon a stone," that is, when the work had not yet been moving forward.

The prophet Haggai speaks to the Jews who returned from exile. They had left the work on the temple stalled for years, busy with their own affairs. God shows them that, without putting Him first, their harvests and efforts were not producing. After this call, the promise is one of blessing (v. 19).

For today: Stop and examine your priorities. If you have left God for last, start again with Him, calmly and sincerely, and trust that He will take care of the rest.
exp.0:10:
God says that He Himself brought drought upon the land. The dryness meant a lack of rain. That drought affected the mountains, the grain, the new wine, the oil, the people, the animals and all the labor of their hands. In other words, nothing they did was bringing them any return.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Haggai, around 520 B.C. The Jews had returned from exile, but they left the rebuilding of the temple abandoned while they built their own houses. God shows them that their scarcity was connected to that wrong priority. Afterward, the people listen, feel reverent fear, and God promises them: "I am with you."

For today: review your priorities. Before you worry about everything that is yours, ask yourself whether you are putting God first. He does not seek to punish you, but to bring you back to Himself.
exp.1:22:
He says that God, on a future day, will take Zerubbabel, his servant, and set him as a signet ring, that is, like the ring with a seal that a king used to sign and authorize documents. The reason is simple: "I have chosen thee." The phrase "will make thee" means "I will make you."

Speaking through the prophet Haggai, the Lord says this around the year 520 B.C. The Jews had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, but they were discouraged. Zerubbabel was the governor and a descendant of David. God promises to shake the kingdoms of the world, and in spite of that he protects Zerubbabel and his line. Some see here a hope that points to the Messiah; the text does not say so in those words.

Even when everything around you is shaken, your worth does not depend on circumstances but on the fact that God chose you. Rest in that and keep serving him faithfully.

sum.0: God speaks through the prophet Haggai and rebukes the people, who were saying that it was not yet the time to rebuild the temple while they themselves were living in luxurious houses. Their harvests and earnings were not producing well because they had put God in second place. The people and their leaders obeyed, God promised them, "I am with you," and they began the work.
sum.1: God encourages Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people to keep rebuilding the temple, even though it looks humble. He promises his presence, his peace, and a future glory greater than the old one. He teaches them that disobedience contaminates what they do, but that from that day on he will bless them. At the end, he promises Zerubbabel that he will choose him like a signet ring.
